speakers: Montesinos Torres, Daniel Borobio Guede, ciudadano chileno
summary: Montesinos meets Daniel Borobio and Gonzalo Menéndez, who represents the Chilean Luksic group and its Lucchetti subsidiary in Peru. Menéndez complains that the factory's construction is blocked by a false environmental report and asks for Montesinos's help. Montesinos tells him to stop dealing through intermediaries such as Vicente Silva or Yoshiyama and to come directly to him, Camet and the Prime Minister, since his involvement guarantees access to the presidency. He telephones judicial contacts during the meeting and arranges to meet again, assuring Menéndez of confidentiality.

The journalist Patricio Ricketts visits Montesinos to ask a personal favour, which Montesinos settles by telephone. The two then talk at length about Sendero Luminoso and the psychology of Abimael Guzmán, with Montesinos attributing the state's victory to coordinated intelligence work and describing a book he says will set his own account beside Guzmán's. Guzmán is discussed throughout but is not present.

Montesinos meets with businessman Julio Vera Abad to discuss the potential secret sale of ATV (Canal 9) to the Military and Police Pension Fund. Vera offers the channel for $10 million, citing personal and legal reasons for the urgent sale, and claims full control over 95% of shares. He presents the channel as a strong asset with national reach and high revenue. Montesinos agrees to evaluate ATV’s finances and legal status before committing. They plan for Montesinos’s team to review the documents at Vera’s residence the next day.

Montesinos and Foreign Minister Eduardo Ferrero discuss maintaining Peru’s military superiority over Ecuador despite recent arms purchases by the latter. Montesinos argues that strong armed forces legitimize the state and sees military strength as essential for political influence, citing Pinochet as an example. Ferrero agrees on prioritizing military preparedness but stresses continued peace negotiations. They also discuss managing negative media coverage, with Montesinos considering influence over journalist Marcelo Gullo. The conversation shifts to the Lori Berenson case, where Montesinos supports a civil trial to appease U.S. concerns while ensuring punishment for terrorism. They agree on forming a trusted security commission and keeping all Ecuador-related strategies confidential, especially before the 1998 elections.

Montesinos reviews Alexander Kouri's recent media appearance for his mayoral campaign, noting a promising 16% polling bump, though critics view his campaign as premature and risky. Kouri shares that he met with Lourdes Flores and warns that Andrade may refuse cooperation if reelected. Montesinos proposes pressuring Andrade to step aside from the 1998 race if he wants support for a 2000 presidential bid. Kouri shifts focus to positive publicity strategies, like promoting public works or a televised fundraiser, and urgently requests 4 million soles to cover Callao's public expenses. Montesinos contacts several officials, confirming Enapu's liquidity and instructing the Viceminister of Transportation to redirect funds to Kouri's administration. After Kouri departs, Montesinos and an aide discuss whether Kouri noticed the hidden video recording equipment.

Part one of a lunch between Montesinos and a representative of the Lucchetti company, recorded on audios 858 and 861. The conversation spans the electoral calendar, the Ecuadorian conflict, Chile, and the army's loyalty to Fujimori, before turning to the company's dispute with Alberto Andrade, the mayor of Lima. The recording ends mid-conversation and continues in transcript 7.

The second half of the Lucchetti lunch begun in transcript 6, recorded on audios 859 and 860. Montesinos reassures his guest that the courts will guarantee the factory's construction, that a judge can grant the urban permit over the municipality's refusal, and that the police will be sent if the works are obstructed. The guest defends the plant against its critics; Montesinos disparages Andrade and sets a date to speak again.

Montesinos meets a man the recording labels “Sr. Americano”, who speaks through an interpreter, together with an unidentified woman. They discuss Baruch Ivcher's campaign in the United States to present his case as a human rights violation, and the Yanacocha mining case, in which Montesinos assures a favourable ruling and dismisses claims of persecution. He hints at reciprocity without naming a price, and they name Ivcher's lawyers and their lobbying contacts in the United States.

The transcriber records that the cassette is largely unusable - most of the text is unintelligible and unable to be attributed to a known participant. What survives is a conversation between Montesinos and an Israeli delegation about defence and surveillance capability, including aerial espionage, and arrangements to meet again once a member of the delegation returns.

Montesinos meets a representative of the Lucchetti company about its dispute with Mayor Andrade over the pasta factory. They coordinate the appeal, with Montesinos guaranteeing a favourable outcome, and discuss how to handle public opinion and the press. Montesinos digresses at length on the state's defeat of terrorism and the embassy hostage rescue. They close by exchanging contacts and with assurances that the case will be resolved shortly.

Congressional and legal leaders meet with Montesinos to plan how to maintain control ahead of the 2000 elections. They discuss judicial appointments, shortening the constitutional accusation procedure, and how to handle Aljovin. Montesinos counts the votes he holds on the Consejo Nacional de la Magistratura and proposes a law granting the Ministerio Publico powers that would otherwise require amending the Constitution. Plans are made to centralise police control under the executive during states of emergency, and Sendero Luminoso and internal threats are cited in support of the measures. Prison conditions, tax cases and press coverage are also discussed.

Montesinos meets an unidentified foreign visitor to discuss recent trips, airplane part shortages and anti-narcotics strategy. They cover the changing tactics of traffickers, air and port surveillance, legislative updates, and training for customs and intelligence staff. Montesinos asks for a meeting with customs officials and stresses the control of informal currency exchanges as a means of limiting money laundering. He describes the private recorded meetings he has held with the imprisoned Sendero Luminoso leader Abimael Guzman and says he intends to broadcast them; a recording of Guzman reading the 1993 peace accord is played during the meeting.

speakers: Barry McCaffrey, Montesinos Torres, Marino Costa, alto mando militar
summary: The American general Barry McCaffrey, his country's anti-drug director, visits Peru and meets Peruvian officials including Montesinos, Hermoza Rios and the United States ambassador. The discussion covers Peru's anti-drug strategy: coca crop reduction, interdiction and alternative development. Montesinos raises the new maritime trafficking route and the coastal cocaine laboratories, and argues for legal reforms to strengthen maritime interdiction and intelligence work. McCaffrey describes Peru's efforts as a regional model and stresses international cooperation. The meeting is followed by a reception, of which the recording captures only fragments of informal conversation.

speakers: Luisa Maria Cuculiza Torre, General EP Briones, Montesinos Torres, Alberto Fujimori
summary: Montesinos and the mayor of San Borja, Maria Luisa Cuculiza Torre, discuss cooperation between the municipality and central government, together with General Briones Davila. They propose a “Ley de la Vagancia” reclassifying petty crime, arguing that judges will not act against street gangs. The conversation covers political positioning, including security initiatives that would weigh against Andrade. Cuculiza requests funds for women's programmes and criticises the limited powers of the Ministry for Women. Fujimori joins later and congratulates her. The SIN's role and the Lucchetti case are mentioned briefly; much of the closing audio is unclear.

speakers: Alipio Montes de Oca, Castillo, Serpa, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos and Supreme Court judge Alipio Montes de Oca discuss judicial reforms and the removal of Jose Dellepiane. Montesinos proposes transferring Montes de Oca to head the Jurado Nacional de Elecciones, offering $10,000 in addition to his salary. The reforms would expedite trials and limit appeals, and both men discuss keeping them in place beyond Fujimori's second term. Serpa and Castillo join later, and all are asked to sign a resolution for publication in El Peruano.

Montesinos meets with José Dellepiane Massa to request his resignation as Executive Secretary of the Comisión Ejecutiva del Poder Judicial, without offering a clear justification. Despite the unexpected nature of the request, Montesinos promises Dellepiane a prestigious post abroad in return, suggesting options like the UN or World Bank. Dellepiane signs a pre-prepared resignation letter, effective in five weeks. Montesinos proposes a formal farewell ceremony, followed by 30 days of paid vacation before Dellepiane assumes his new international role.

Montesinos meets Supreme Court Justice Jaime Beltran Quiroga, a former classmate, about the Yanacocha mining dispute between the Peruvian-US consortium Newmont-Buenaventura and the French company BRGM. Montesinos stresses what he presents as the geopolitical stakes, citing United States involvement through the Rio de Janeiro Protocol and the need to preserve relations with Ecuador before its elections, and argues that the national interest lies with Newmont-Buenaventura. Much of the remaining conversation concerns their shared schooling in Arequipa and appointments within the judiciary.

speakers: Denis Jett, Marino Costa, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos, Health Minister Costa Bauer, and U.S. Ambassador Dennis Jett meet to ease tensions caused by a controversial TV broadcast about General McCaffrey’s visit. Costa clarifies that the segment was independently edited and urges a joint statement to reaffirm cooperation. Montesinos agrees, emphasizing Peru’s strong counter-narcotics ties with the U.S. and proposing reforms to money laundering laws, real-time bank monitoring, and improved protections for undercover agents. He also suggests legal changes to clarify maritime enforcement roles. Ambassador Jett remains cautious but agrees to explore a public statement. Montesinos proposes a symbolic appearance with President Fujimori to reinforce diplomatic unity. The meeting ends with light conversation and birthday wishes.

Montesinos meets Health Minister Costa Bauer to plan anti-narcotics legislation, and later receives the Chilean admiral Patricio Arancibia, accompanied by another Chilean officer, with the Peruvian admiral Ibarcena present. Costa Bauer proposes reforms to the money laundering laws; Montesinos recommends decrees on banking surveillance, naval interdiction and media control, and they coordinate a response to press coverage of tensions with the United States, including a possible joint appearance with the ambassador. With Arancibia the conversation turns to military modernisation, secrecy, the press, Pinochet, and operations such as Chavin de Huantar.

speakers: Santander, Javier Valle Riestra Gonzales Olaechea, Montesinos Torres.
summary: Montesinos and Prime Minister Valle Riestra discuss national reconstruction and the pressures on stability from El Nino, unemployment and the state of the judiciary. Montesinos defends the counter-terrorism measures of the period, including military tribunals, as necessary to the survival of the state, and describes the unacknowledged work of intelligence officers in contrast to that of politicians. Montesinos offers guidance as Valle Riestra begins his term. They agree that his first act will be the release of 30 wrongly convicted prisoners, with further policy discussions to follow.

Montesinos and Santander, advisor to Prime Minister Valle Riestra, discuss budgeting issues at OSPITEL, where Valle Riestra wants increased compensation for advisors. Montesinos insists budget changes are unconstitutional due to OSPITEL’s regulatory status. They also plan to reframe Valle Riestra’s public image as a flexible and supportive Prime Minister who advances Fujimori’s agenda. Topics include unemployment, crime, judicial reform, and national reconstruction. Santander pledges loyalty to Montesinos and Fujimori, and they plan a follow-up meeting to coordinate national strategies.

Montesinos and Valle Riestra discuss a proposed referendum on Fujimori's reelection, with Montesinos arguing that voters are more concerned with employment than with constitutional questions. He asks Valle Riestra to support the national reconstruction plan and to lead judicial reform. Valle Riestra, who opposes reelection, observes that Fujimori's rivals are weak, and Montesinos tells him the referendum will not pass. The conversation turns to foreign policy, in particular settling the conflict with Ecuador so that attention can return to domestic matters.

speakers: Garcia Marcelo, Hernandez Canelo, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos meets with Magistrates José García Marcelo and Walter Hernández to influence a resolution by ONPE regarding a potential 2000 referendum. They debate constitutional interpretations to delay or block the referendum process, favoring congressional control. Montesinos stresses the need to marginalize ONPE’s role and anticipates opposition from Lourdes Flores and Javier Diez Canseco. He also briefly addresses national unity in response to Ecuadorian military tensions, noting the importance of political stability ahead of Peru’s upcoming presidential transition.

speakers: Medelius Rodrigo, Romulo Munoz, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos meets Congressman Oscar Medelius and Romulo Munoz Arce of the JNE to work out a legal strategy against a referendum on Fujimori's reelection. They examine Article 44 of the Constitution as a basis for arguing that the referendum could threaten national security, and discuss the ONPE and JNE timetables and how the process might be blocked or delayed on constitutional and procedural grounds. Timing is coordinated around Ecuador's presidential transition. A fourth participant speaks throughout but is never identified in the recording.

Montesinos is decorated by the Air Force with its highest distinction for his counter-terrorism role. In his speech he praises work done out of public view and recalls past operations against traffickers and subversion. The group discusses judicial reforms to expedite minor criminal cases and reduce police corruption. Montesinos sets out the mechanics of a referendum on Fujimori's reelection and the constitution, referring to Articles 31 and 17, and describes the legal routes available.

speakers: Borobio Guede, Hurtado Miller, Montesinos Torres
summary: Hurtado Miller and Borobio critique rival Andrade’s aloof public image while plotting to rebrand Hurtado as a relatable, action-oriented candidate. They focus on the symbolic use of a tractor to represent hard work and resilience. Highlighting Andrade’s failure to address key public concerns, they aim to position Hurtado as an experienced administrator with social sensitivity. The conversation stresses the importance of loyal journalists like Nicolás Lúcar and pre-arranged interview questions. Montesinos briefly joins to listen as the team plans early debates and discusses how to deflect questions on the referendum. They aim to flood media coverage with coordinated attacks and relatable messaging.

speakers: Juan Carlos Hurtado Miller, Montesinos Torres.
summary: Montesinos funds Juan Carlos Hurtado Miller’s campaign with $215,000, two vehicles, and staff, stressing the importance of media control and public visibility. He encourages Hurtado to blend into large rallies and downplay elitist imagery. Borobio critiques Hurtado’s physical appearance and messaging, recommending dental work and a new campaign slogan involving a tractor symbol. They agree to delay a major speech to avoid clashing with the announcement of the new Prime Minister. The meeting covers detailed media coordination, polling strategy, and a push to dominate public discourse with pro-government narratives. Hurtado and Borobio later meet with Montesinos to review campaign photos and a packed calendar of events.

Montesinos and Victor Joy Way plot to block a constitutional referendum that would limit Fujimori’s reelection. They orchestrate bribes of $3,000 monthly to secure votes in Congress and judicial bodies, focusing on controlling electoral rulings. They express concern over one holdout, Ferrero, and discuss how to sway or isolate him. Their broader strategy includes buying media outlets and flooding coverage with pro-government propaganda, especially through print and TV channels. The plan includes legal maneuvers in the JNE, pushing a resolution to override constitutional restrictions. Media control is central, and budget constraints lead them to redirect funds from Hurtado Miller’s campaign to cover propaganda.

speakers: General EP Hermoza Rios, General EP Villanueva Ruesta, General PNP Dianderas O, General FAP Elesban Vello, Almirante Ibarcena, General EP Salazar Monroe, General EP Saucedo, Montesinos Torres, Alberto Fujimori
summary: President Fujimori announces that General Saucedo will replace Hermoza Rios as Commander General of the Army, ending a six-year tenure. After the announcement, Montesinos and Saucedo telephone military commanders to inform them of the change and invite them to an event, and discuss practical matters such as official vehicles. Saucedo has difficulty reaching some of them. Fujimori speaks of institutional continuity and Hermoza gives a farewell address.

speakers: Antonio Ibárcena, Alex Kouri, Francisco Kouri, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos, Alex Kouri and Admiral Ibarcena discuss Francisco Kouri's cooperation in his drug case, with the aim of reclassifying it as personal consumption and avoiding a prison term. Kouri then reports that Andrade's party, Somos Peru, has filed a formal challenge -- a tacha -- against the ballot symbol of his own movement, Chim Pum Callao, and has appealed so that the case rises to the Jurado Nacional de Elecciones. Montesinos says he has contacts at the JNE and will see that the challenge does not prosper. Kouri also asks for the head of CORDELICA to be removed in order to strengthen his position in Callao.

Montesinos, Kouri, and Admiral Ibárcena coordinate damage control over corruption leaks in Callao and plan a media campaign against Lima Mayor Andrade. Montesinos promises legal protection and orchestrates a three-part media strategy involving government statements, TV appearances, and narrative control. They aim to frame Kouri as transparent and Andrade as deceitful. The conversation ends with confirmation that Francisco Kouri will cooperate legally, securing him potential leniency.

Montesinos and Mayor Alex Kouri engage in a relaxed conversation covering personal anecdotes, political gossip, and Kouri’s travel ambitions. Kouri discusses avoiding scandal as a public figure, criticizes Martha Chávez’s investigations into government trips, and shares frustrations with political rivals, including his own family and Mayor Andrade. The conversation briefly touches on CORDELICA appointments and ends with Kouri describing his evening community outreach work as Montesinos arrives.

speakers: Luis Venero Garrido, Ernesto Gamarra Olivares, Roberto Huaman Azcurra, Manuel Tafur Ruiz
summary: Luis Venero Garrido rehearses with Huaman Azcurra how to hand over a payment to Congressman Ernesto Gamarra Olivares. Gamarra arrives, accepts a suitcase of cash, and discusses using media influence to move attention away from the Venero family, in particular his brother Victor and the arms dealings attributed to him. Manuel Tafur Ruiz is also present and speaks.

President Fujimori instructs Congressman Jorge Trelles to meet Ecuadorian President Jamil Mahuad and promote a peace agreement within 90 days. They discuss gaining congressional support while condemning opposition voices like Carlos Ferrero, who publicly criticized the peace effort. Fujimori receives a call from Mahuad and confirms a vote will occur the next day, aiming for a unified message from Peru’s government.

speakers: Vera Gutiérrez, Borobio, Julio Vera, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos and Borobio meet the ATV executive Julio Vera Gutierrez and hand over cash reported as $50,000 in exchange for favourable television coverage. Vera Gutierrez agrees to dismiss critical journalists, among them Cecilia Valenzuela, and to replace opposition voices with figures friendly to the government. They discuss a special programme on relations with Ecuador, drawing on advance knowledge of Fujimori's forthcoming address to Congress, and agree to coordinate programming every ten days.

Montesinos hands the television executive Jose Francisco Crousillat Carreno 1,857,000 soles, which he states is the equivalent of $619,000, as payment for coverage favouring Fujimori. The sum is prorated over the period from October 1998 to July 1999. Crousillat had expected payment in dollars; Montesinos explains that he is paying in soles because the money is needed immediately, and offers to convert the next instalment. He stresses the need to present Fujimori's reconstruction programmes favourably, and proposes agreeing a further commitment for 2000 to 2005 on 28 July 2000. The conversation closes with small talk about family holidays and future meetings.

Montesinos, Munoz Arce and Medelius Rodriguez discuss correcting voter registration errors from the October municipal elections in preparation for 2000. They propose reforms to reduce double-counting and criticise preferential voting. The conversation then turns to personal matters: Montesinos offers $30,000 towards the education of Munoz Arce's daughter in the United States, and job placements for his son and wife. The growing political presence of the MRTA is mentioned briefly.

Montesinos and Rómulo Muñoz Arce discuss a TV broadcast by journalist César Hildebrandt, who is critical of the regime. They agree on pressuring media outlets to silence him. Montesinos arranges a first-class flight and customs assistance for Muñoz’s daughter. They also discuss voting ID verification issues, proposing measures to prevent homonymy and ensure more accurate voter registration.

Manuel Guillen, newly elected mayor of Arequipa, visits the SIN with an adviser at Montesinos's invitation. Montesinos returns repeatedly to their shared Arequipa origins, and the discussion ranges over the city's universities, schools and development. Guillen argues for municipal responsibility in primary education and notes his party's critical stance toward the government.

speakers: Montesinos Torres, General EP Villanueva Ruesta, Oficiales EP
summary: Montesinos and General Villanueva discuss military backing for Fujimori's reelection. They devise a media strategy associating the colour yellow with Sendero Luminoso in order to damage an opposing campaign. Montesinos then meets a series of officers individually, telling each that he is to be promoted to General, praising his professionalism and loyalty, and instructing him to keep the news confidential until later that week.

speakers: Montesino Torres, General EP Villanueva Ruesta, Oficiales EP
summary: Montesinos and General Villanueva Ruesta meet a succession of colonels individually to tell each that he is to be promoted to General, citing loyalty and competence, and instructing him to say nothing until Friday. Montesinos states repeatedly that he and Villanueva are the deciding authorities, above the Minister of the Interior. Some officers are also given specific tasks, such as looking into requests for expanded media bandwidth.

Montesinos tries to quash rumors about the arrest of General Hermoza Ríos, who has allegedly been abroad for medical treatment. He drafts a memo denying the arrest and plans media coverage to reinforce the official story. Congressman Carlos Ferrero visits, expressing surprise at receiving a holiday gift and voicing concern about being sidelined politically. Montesinos claims it was due to congressional preferences but shares inside information about the Hermoza situation. Ferrero warns of the need to rethink opposition strategy before the 2000 election and urges better management of human rights and electoral decentralization. Montesinos later discusses press payments and plans to release new messaging during January’s commemorative events.

speakers: Joy Way Rojas, Maria Cuculiza Torre, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos meets with Congressmember Joy Way and Mayor Luisa María Cuculiza, urging her to publicly denounce her former party leader, Andrade, to disassociate from Somos Perú. He offers her a ministerial role in women’s affairs as a political reward. Though Cuculiza resists initially, she agrees to align with Fujimori’s strategy, aiming for future congressional leadership. Both criticize opposition figure Carlos Ferrero.

speakers: Jose Francisco Crousillat, Montesinos Torres, Gisela Valcarcel, Jose Enrique Crouisillat
summary: Montesinos advises Gisela Valcarcel to sue the author Carlos Vidal for defamation and moral damages in order to block publication of a book about her private life, presenting the case as a precedent for protecting women's dignity in public life. The conversation then turns to counter-terrorism and espionage, including Chile's use of marriages for intelligence purposes and Montesinos's own disciplinary measures, and to the MRTA hostage crisis and the preparation for military intervention alongside the handling of the press. After Valcarcel leaves, Montesinos and the two Crousillats turn to America Television's finances. Crousillat Lopez Torres asks him to intervene with Banco Wiese, and Montesinos agrees to arrange the meeting.

speakers: General EP Salazar Monroe, General EP Villanueva, General EP Saucedo, Almirante Ibarcena Amico, General FAP Bello Vasquez, General PNP Dianderas, Contralmirante Rosas, Oficiales FFAA, Oficiales PNP, Montesinos Torres
summary: The armed forces leadership meets to record its support for the 1992 self-coup and to reject accusations of human rights violations. Speakers credit the coup with the defeat of terrorism and narcotrafficking and invoke the amnesty laws covering military personnel. They object to recent press criticism and undertake to protect those involved in past operations. The Baruch Ivcher case is presented as a campaign against the armed forces, with Ivcher said to have compromised national security. Communications on the case are classified, and those present sign the session's conclusions into the record.

speakers: General EP Salazar Monroe, General EP Villanueva, General EP Saucedo, Almirante Ibarcena Amico, General FAP Bello Vasquez, General PNP Dianderas, Contralmirante Rosas, Oficiales FFAA, Oficiales PNP, Montesinos Torres
summary: Senior military and police officers meet to defend the 1992 self-coup and their conduct during the MRTA hostage rescue. Accusations of human rights violations are rejected, with speakers invoking the amnesty laws and describing critics as unpatriotic. The session includes anthems and patriotic declarations. The Baruch Ivcher case is again raised as a threat to national security, with earlier documents confirming surveillance and non-disclosure. Those present are warned that breaking confidentiality would be a dishonourable offence, and all are recorded and asked to sign the session's strictly secret act.

speakers: Victor Joy Way, Genaro Delgado Parker
summary: Victor Joy Way and Genaro Delgado Parker meet without Montesinos, who does not take part in this conversation. Delgado Parker reviews his career in Peruvian media and telecommunications and his legal disputes with his brothers Manuel and Hector over control of the companies. He speaks well of his relationship with Crousillat and mentions Cesar Hildebrandt's contract, which permits dismissal without cause. Joy Way urges him to dismiss Hildebrandt, and Delgado Parker asks for help in advancing his court cases.

speakers: Victor Joy Way, Delgado Parker, Montesinos Torres
summary: Genaro Delgado Parker asks Montesinos for help in his legal disputes with his brothers over the telecommunications company BellSouth and ownership of Panamericana TV. He recounts earlier business successes and describes the position his family has left him in. Montesinos agrees to support him, citing his past service to the armed forces, and suspends a notification to give him time. They discuss media consolidation, with Delgado Parker proposing mergers. Montesinos presses him to dismiss the journalist Hildebrandt or bind him to a stricter contract. Delgado Parker also raises a proposal to form an anti-narcotics NGO in Miami with United States support.

speakers: Eduardo Calmell Del Solar, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos discusses instability in Latin America and describes Peru as the United States' closest ally against terrorism, drug trafficking and weapons of mass destruction. He praises Fujimori's leadership and the anti-narcotics laws, and returns to Baruch Ivcher, accusing him of using politics and the media for personal gain. He offers Eduardo Calmell financial backing for El Expreso in exchange for support for Fujimori's reelection. Calmell says he will consider the offer and reply within days.

speakers: Eduardo Calmell Del Solar, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos and Eduardo Calmell del Solar settle the terms on which Calmell will support the government's media strategy over the next twelve to fifteen months. Montesinos asks for a reporter to accompany a forthcoming trip to Colombia, and Calmell offers Jorge Morelli. They also discuss pressing Emilio Rodriguez Larrain to drop his defence of Baruch Ivcher, the owner of Canal 2, who had been stripped of his Peruvian nationality.

Genaro Delgado Parker thanks Montesinos for extending a deadline and for financial support during his legal difficulties. He asks for help with two cases: one concerning alleged misuse of influence in a cable television deal, the other his daughter's exposure in a divorce. They then discuss founding an NGO in Miami to assist United States counter-narcotics work using Latin American intelligence. Montesinos describes Peru's cooperation as essential, citing operations against Islamic fundamentalists and traffickers, and proposes border security measures in anticipation of possible United States military action in Colombia. He states that future presidents will have to negotiate with the armed forces and the intelligence services.

speakers: Alamo Perez, Alberto Fujimori, Montesinos Torres
summary: A joint interview with Montesinos and Fujimori conducted by the journalist Alamo Perez Luna about the MRTA hostage crisis, recorded by the SIN's own camera. Fujimori stresses the search for a peaceful settlement and his personal direction of the intelligence work. Montesinos says surveillance and timing were decisive in the rescue, and describes the SIN renting nearby houses to watch the MRTA and paying the owners to keep the press away. He states that he ordered the assault once the captors' positions had been confirmed. The recording captures exchanges on the set that were cut before broadcast.

speakers: Luis Bedoya de Vivanco, Reategui, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos plans an economic paper presenting Peru as the United States' principal ally in Latin America on counter-narcotics and counter-terrorism, and assesses Andrade and Castaneda as weak rivals. Meeting Luis Bedoya de Vivanco, who is standing for mayor of Miraflores, he offers voter data, media access and advice on how to undercut Jaime Salinas, and they agree to present a vote for Salinas as a wasted vote. Montesinos advises against using Channel 7, which would make their coordination visible, and recommends frequent appearances in the news.

speakers: Comandantes Generales, Dionisio Romero, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos tells Dionisio Romero that only Fujimori has the military backing needed to govern, and dismisses his rivals. Romero warns that overconfidence may rebound on them and proposes changes to the economic message and to the slate of candidates. Montesinos says poll results can be bought for $10,000. They discuss a highway project intended to raise Fujimori's standing and whether to replace the Minister of Economy; Romero declines a cabinet post and suggests Jorge Camet. They plan interviews presenting Andrade as better suited to the mayoralty than the presidency.

speakers: Luis Bedoya de Vivanco, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos, Bedoya and Gonzales Reategui review favourable polling for Bedoya in the Miraflores mayoral race. They plan media attacks on Alberto Andrade around a construction failure linked to him, scheduling coverage across several television and radio channels. Montesinos gives Bedoya $25,000 for campaign use, against a receipt. They discuss a late “lost vote” campaign. Bedoya sets out a neighbourhood security plan using dogs rather than firearms and paid citizen reporting, supported by a proposed Office for the Safety of Citizens, which Montesinos agrees to promote as a cheaper alternative to the existing serenazgo.

Montesinos and banker Dionisio Romero discuss shifting political focus from declining candidate Andrade to rising contender Castaneda Lossio. They analyse Castaneda's recent mistakes and criticise Andrade's missed opportunity to partner with Fujimori. Romero requests a wheat tariff reduction to lower bread prices. On Colombia, Montesinos says the United States should have the country's own armed forces stage a coup.

speakers: Luis Bedoya de Vivanco, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos congratulates Bedoya, saying that adverse publicity around Andrade has improved Bedoya's standing, and speaks of Miraflores as a step toward the Lima mayoralty. He says 1,500 patrol vehicles are due to arrive within two to three months for distribution nationwide, with some 600 to 700 remaining in Lima, and says he will see that some go to Miraflores to reinforce its police stations. A later section of the recording, from the second video, captures two men arranging photocopies and discussing travel schedules; a stage direction describes them only as unidentified.

speakers: Victor Joy Way, Bustamente, Gross, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos and senior officials discuss fast-tracking a legal report through Cabinet and Congress before July 11. Montesinos warns of 80 upcoming trials, including politically sensitive cases like Lori Berenson, Baruch Ivcher, and alleged phone surveillance, which may trigger public controversy.

speakers: Montesinos Torres, Embajador, General EP Villanueva Ruesta, General EP Bergamino
summary: Montesinos and the United States ambassador work through final changes to an anti-narcotics cooperation agreement, strengthening the language on sanctions. Montesinos sets out the constraints imposed by Peruvian law, the budget and the standards of evidence required before penalties can be applied. After the ambassador leaves, Villanueva and Bergamino discuss the distinction between national and international accords and which framework should cover conflict resolution and disaster response.

Montesinos discusses the arrest of the Sendero Luminoso leader Feliciano, contrasting him with Abimael Guzman. A negotiation follows over the restructuring of Banco de Comercio debt, with Eugenio Bertini, a childhood friend of Montesinos, advising on credit lines and warning against property guarantees. Crousillat Lopez Torres is present, as is a fourth man the recording identifies only as “Sr. WO”. The conversation turns to media strategy, Laura Bozzo's ratings and a planned public appearance with Fujimori, and to Bedoya's reliability and Andrade's declining support.

Montesinos meets United States officials, with Humberto Rozas of the SIN present, to discuss the second phase of an anti-drug agreement. He objects to imprecise wording on institutional responsibility and sets out the legal limits of state liability. The conversation moves to Latin American politics, with Montesinos predicting a return of military governments across the region, pointing to instability in Colombia and Ecuador, and doubting that democratic rule will hold into the next decade.

speakers: General EP Bergamino, General EP Saucedo, General EP Villanueva, Almirante Ibarcena, General FAP Elesban Bello, General PNP Dianderas, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos meets the service commanders to plan changes in the high command and amendments to the Ley de Situacion Militar limiting commanders' tenure while preserving rank after retirement. General Saucedo is to become Minister of the Interior and Army Commander in place of Villanueva, who is to be honoured publicly. Montesinos warns that the reelection campaign will bring press attacks on the armed forces and urges unity. They also discuss the distribution of United States aid, which they regard as favouring Colombia and Bolivia over Peru, and a proposal to form a civilian association representing those displaced by the conflict.

speakers: Montesinos Torres, Representante de Estados Unidos, Heather
summary: Montesinos meets representatives of the United States embassy on counter-narcotics cooperation. The American ambassador recounts having told the press of her concern over human rights abuses and corruption in anti-narcotics units; Montesinos replies that there is nothing of the kind. He then presses for a money-laundering law, arguing that investigations stall because SUNAT will not release tax information without a lifting of bank secrecy.

Montesinos, Manuel Delgado Parker and Ernesto Schutz discuss controlling Laura Bozzo's airtime and criticise the Crousillats' handling of their finances, with Canal 4 carrying $160 million of debt. Delgado Parker asks for help in several court cases; Montesinos declines to pay judges, saying it would set a costly precedent. They discuss Andrade's declining support and a target of 44% of the vote by December, and treat El Comercio's reporting on corruption at the SIN as a deliberate attack. They plan a media campaign promoting the government and criticising opposition figures including Hildebrandt.

speakers: Defensor del Pueblo, General EP Villanueva Ruesta, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos discusses Shining Path cases with ombudsman Jorge Santistevan, stressing humane treatment while referencing interactions with Abimael Guzmán. He proposes civilian-led intelligence reforms and defends SIN against media accusations linked to forged documents, such as Plan Octavio. Montesinos claims these fabrications aim to frame SIN for persecuting journalists. The conversation ends with an unclear request for a favor.

speakers: Eduardo Calmell Del Solar, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos invites Eduardo Calmell to a military ceremony and discusses the loyalty of particular outlets. He says Genaro Delgado Parker may withdraw his support from Andrade, and that 1,500 patrol vehicles will arrive in December, of which about 300 will go to Lima and 50 to Callao. He hands Calmell a payment and undertakes to provide the remainder on Friday.

speakers: Eduardo Calmell Del Solar, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos and Calmell discuss claims made in Congress about Interpol's role in the Ivcher case and complain of politicised press coverage. Montesinos dismisses Ivcher as no longer relevant and says United States interest rests solely with Fujimori. He hands Calmell the remaining $500,000 from their earlier arrangement, counting it out, and refers to a further $3,000 a month in support.

speakers: General Delgado, Vicente Silva, Eduardo Calmell, Vladimiro Montesinos
summary: Vicente Silva hesitates to acquire CCN shares due to needing his wife's consent and the covert nature of the deal. Montesinos gives him $2 million and grants time to resolve it. The group later discusses the financial state of major banks and praises Victor Joy Way for his economic management.

Montesinos tells Domingo Palermo that Fujimori will stand for reelection and asks for the channel's support. He objects to particular journalists, beginning with Beto Ortiz. Palermo sets out his plans, saying he is renewing the whole political section and has recruited staff identified with Fujimori, and runs through their names and backgrounds; he states that he has never been disloyal. Montesinos suggests attacking opponents indirectly and praises Guido Lombardi's handling of media disputes.

Bertini reports that Banco Wiese's position has improved since the intervention and attributes its earlier difficulties to the Wiese family's management. Montesinos asks about other banks and is told that Banex is close to bankruptcy while the rest are stable. Bertini offers offshore banking in Panama and the Cayman Islands and proposes setting up a company through which deposits could be held. They discuss the finances of Canal 2 and Canal 4 and the number of television channels being put up for sale. Samuel Winter Zuzunaga and Crousillat Lopez Torres join the conversation, looking for new investors. Bertini says the Peruvian financial sector carries too much debt and too little capital for a quick recovery.

speakers: General Villanueva, Almirante Ibarcena, General Bello
summary: Montesinos and the service commanders plan the Dia del Ejercito as a display of unity and of anti-narcotics capability. Montesinos says a Plan 2005 is being drawn up in secret with Bolona to prepare for the period after Fujimori's term ends, and observes that Bolona's emergence gives him a rival for 2005. They set out a publicity approach built on warnings about security, television specials, mass events and attacks on rival candidates, including re-running on Canal 4 the specials Laura Bozzo made about terrorism. Montesinos also lists gifts he has been given.

speakers: General Villanueva, Almirante Ibarcena, General Bello, Winter
summary: Montesinos praises El Expreso and plans to mass-publish a report showcasing Peru’s progress under Fujimori. He and Boloña discuss economic strategy and media control for the 2005 election. The group also coordinates military promotions, which will take effect immediately after public announcement on December 10.

Enrique Chirinos offers to support Fujimori in Congress in exchange for a favorable spot on the electoral list, campaign funds, and media space. Montesinos agrees, promising TV ads, a campaign office, and meetings with Fujimori. They discuss broader political strategy, including targeting Castañeda and ensuring a congressional majority.

Montesinos urges Ketin Vidal to accept a vice-presidential candidacy focused on internal security. Vidal expresses reluctance due to media scrutiny and personal priorities, particularly fearing journalist Hildebrandt. Montesinos insists he is ideal for the role and encourages him to decide by 6 p.m., claiming everything is ready for his appointment.

Vidal formally declines Montesinos's offer of the vice-presidency, citing his family and press scrutiny. He affirms his loyalty to Fujimori and says he will not join the opposition. The exchange is cordial and both agree to stay in touch. The conversation took place on Christmas Day.

speakers: Alex Kouri Bumachar, Jose Francisco Crousillat, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos meets with Alex Kouri and José Francisco Crousillat to discuss political strategy. They reflect on recent Peru 2000 protests, with Crousillat arguing police restraint prevented greater bloodshed. Kouri affirms his loyalty to Fujimori and proposes a symbolic gesture of unity on International Wetlands Day. He shares ambitions for a future presidential run, which Montesinos says should follow success in the 2002 municipal elections. Both express disappointment with Andrade.

Montesinos and Kouri strategize for the upcoming election, noting poll shifts: Castañeda has overtaken Andrade in second place. With only 56 days left, they agree to refocus attacks on Castañeda. Kouri reports advice to move faster but remains cautious. They plan to revisit Andrade in the 2002 mayoral race after securing the presidency.

speakers: Osmán Morote, María Pantoja, Montesinos Torres
summary: Montesinos reprimands the prison officials Morote and Pantoja after a Sendero Luminoso riot at Yanamayo. He orders the physical evidence cleared, care for injured staff and inmates, and no press coverage, and tells the general in charge that no record is to be drawn up and nothing signed. He repeats that compliance is needed to avoid a reaction. Pantoja joins the call, confirming communication problems, and they discuss Feliciano, whom Montesinos indicates has changed sides and about whom he says surprising news will follow.

Montesinos gives Agustin Mantilla Campos $30,000 for his campaign in a short meeting. They discuss Jorge del Castillo, whom Montesinos calls dangerous but not worth acting against, expecting his position to weaken. Montesinos says he has instructed Canal 2, Canal 4 and Canal 7 to give Mantilla more airtime. Further collaboration in 2005 is mentioned.

Montesinos apologises to Kouri for not having been in touch. Kouri describes the reaction to his remarks on Radio Programas about Toledo and Salas, which they had agreed in advance, and says Salas's weak campaign is helping Toledo, particularly in Chimbote. Concerned about a second round, they discuss securing loyal congressional candidates. They agree a publicity line: that the mayor of Callao has obtained $45 million without adding to the municipality's debt. They also plan an event at the Real Felipe fortress with ambassadors invited, and debate whether to hold it on the 29th or the 30th.

Montesinos and others plan their communications around Semana Santa, expecting little public attention over the religious holiday. They hold messaging back and concentrate on discrediting Alejandro Toledo, discussing how his candidacy might be invalidated and agreeing to draft a document and bring a legal action. Montesinos warns that outlets may turn against the government if they feel abandoned, and payments to maintain their support are discussed.

Montesinos meets senior officers to plan for the 2000 presidential runoff. They discuss payments to congressmen, the handling of vote tallies, and the redirection of intelligence funds towards the press and the courts. Monthly contributions from the services are to fund publicity, including the chicha tabloids. They coordinate their response to the Salazar torture case and review military readiness. Montesinos goes through the arrangements in detail, down to seating and the wording to be used. Relations with foreign embassies are also discussed.

Montesinos describes intelligence networks in Colombia, with agents in place for years and producing, he says, better material than the United States receives. He recounts being ordered to execute Abimael Guzman in 1992 and delaying it in order to trace the finances of the insurgency, and says he went on to build a rapport with Guzman and to record thousands of hours of their conversations. He voices concern about the future of the armed forces, and Tudela tells him his own position is essential to them.

Montesinos negotiates the defection of Congressman-elect Alberto Kouri from Peru Posible to Peru 2000. Kouri explains that he intends to resign discreetly, citing his exclusion within the party, and wants it to appear a matter of principle rather than opportunism. Montesinos stresses that Kouri must be aligned by August in order to affect congressional votes, particularly the election of new leadership. They agree a payment of $15,000 for Kouri's campaign costs, with further support through intermediaries. They also discuss recruiting further defectors and using local programmes in Callao to build support. The defection is to take place after the congressional transition on 28 July.

Montesinos discusses the torture of a man who had obtained several of the recordings, understood to be the journalist Fabian Salazar. He rejects the man's account and sets out how to discredit him publicly, with material to be broadcast through friendly outlets. The conversation turns to Baruch Ivcher and Canal 2, and to placing coverage on Canal 4's Hora 20. Long silences run through the recording, with a television tuned to Canal N audible throughout.

Montesinos convenes a meeting with police and military officials to plan a crackdown on post-election opposition activity, especially targeting Alejandro Toledo. He instructs prefects to deny permits for political gatherings, arguing they are now illegal. Plans are made to deploy covert operatives posing as civilians to disrupt rallies, while security forces remain hidden but ready. Tactics include disabling vehicles, deploying gas grenades, and using psychological warfare to demoralize opponents. Surveillance is ordered on political figures and events in Arequipa, with legal cover arranged through preemptive documentation. Control over media and public access to state events is also prioritized. Montesinos underscores the need for unified action between the Armed Forces and National Police.

Montesinos pays the Panamericana TV executive Ernesto Schutz, with Victor Joy Way present. A stage direction records Montesinos taking out three bundles of $100,000, one of $40,000 and one of $10,000, making $350,000 in all. Schutz raises the property disputes and court pressure he faces, and Montesinos assures him of protection from SUNAT and IPSS from January. They plan staged interviews with former Sendero Luminoso members and coverage presenting Fujimori favourably. Montesinos promises encrypted telephones and says he can direct judges, journalists and channels, naming Hildebrandt and Canal 13. They also discuss working against political opponents and using the OAS and the Castillo Petruzzi case to argue for wider state powers.

Montesinos urges Francisco Tudela not to stand for president of Congress, citing the instability he expects. He recommends Martha Hildebrandt as a loyal but neutral alternative. Tudela criticises Beatriz Boza's leadership of PromPeru and suggests she be removed. Both treat Baruch Ivcher as a serious threat and discuss forcing him out of Canal 2, including having military spokesmen attack him in state media.

Side one of tape 351-A. Montesinos and Carlos Boloña go over arrangements for a military coup planned for that week, naming the officials to be kept on and the opponents to be detained. The audio is badly degraded and much of it is marked unintelligible. At least three people are present, and a stage direction records Montesinos leaving the room and returning. Transcript 90 is the other side of the same tape.

speakers: Funcionario del Banco Wiese, Montesinos Torres
summary: Side two of tape 351-A, holding two conversations separated by a break in the recording. In the first, Montesinos and Carlos Boloña continue planning the coup, settling the swearing-in at Palacio and who will place the presidential sash. After the tape cut, Montesinos turns to personal banking with an unnamed Banco Wiese official: credit-card limits for his wife and daughter, and the handling of accounts abroad. Transcript 89 is the other side of the same tape.

speakers: Luis Frank Aybar Cancho, José Manuel López Rodríguez, Rhaquel Granda, Del Mar Colina
summary: A video record of a State Security operation, narrated on camera by a woman's voice and a man's voice, with a prosecutor present. Officers search the house in Chaclacayo and Chosica where the detained Luis Frank Aybar Cancho and Juan Manuel Lopez Rodriguez had been hiding, accused of supplying weapons to the FARC, recovering documents, identity papers, mobile telephones and foreign passports. Rhaquel Granda Zapata is questioned about sheltering the suspects and about moving them between addresses. Lopez Rodriguez is questioned and describes himself as a Spanish business adviser. A further search at Jose Alejandro Del Mar Colina's home turns up papers connecting him to Japanese companies and to an Air Force general, together with a hunting shotgun. A vehicle used in the case is registered to a company called Sistemas Estrategicos Financieros S.A.

speakers: Jose Luis, Luis Frank Aybar Cancho
summary: A video record of a State Security operation, narrated on camera by a woman's voice. The recording opens with a tour of the homes of those accused of trafficking arms to the FARC, then follows the search of the house of Victor Ivachine, a Russian national dealing in arms and connected to the staff of his embassy in Lima. Officers recover documents, passports, video tapes and a police vest found in a vehicle Ivachine says he bought second-hand. He is questioned about his mining interests, his background in aviation and his dealings with Luis Aybar, whom he describes as a business partner. Surveillance footage shows him meeting people connected to the Russian embassy, including several vehicles with diplomatic plates. Ivachine is detained, his personal details are formally recorded, and he is taken to State Security offices.

speakers: Raquel Smith de Lopez, Smith, Flor
summary: A video record of a State Security operation, narrated on camera. Officers search the home of Juan Manuel Lopez Rodriguez, a Spanish national and business partner of the Aybar Cancho brothers, accused of trafficking arms to the FARC. He had left the house shortly before and was not found there. His wife, Enna Raquel Smith Maguina de Lopez, is questioned throughout the search. The search of the house and of vehicles registered to the family turns up a range of personal items and documents, but no contraband. Further footage covers surveillance and secondary inspections at other properties.

speakers: Liliana Villarreal, Arnulfo Alvarado, Luis Frank Aybar
summary: A video record of the arraignment and transfer of those detained under Plan Siberia for trafficking arms to the FARC, narrated on camera. Over several days in early September the detainees, among them Victor Ivachine, Luis Frank Aybar Cancho, Liliana Villarreal Landeo and Juan Manuel Lopez Rodriguez, are brought from the DININCRI cells to a judicial chamber where their personal details are formally recorded and the charges put to them. Each signs documents and is fingerprinted before returning to the cells. On 25 September the men are moved to Castro Castro prison and the women, including Villarreal Landeo, to Chorrillos, in a convoy of police and intelligence vehicles tracked by radio across Lima. The detainees are filmed with their faces covered as they are taken into the prisons.

Montesinos and an unidentified associate discuss vote manipulation, payments and the movement of money through several banks. They set out the use of offshore accounts and arrangements for holding large sums in safe houses. They discuss placing people in legal institutions and in SUNAT in order to influence the courts. They speak dismissively of demonstrators against Fujimori and stress the need to control coverage, and note that conversations are being recorded for later use. Montesinos says he distrusts his associates and that only his daughter is to know the arrangements for leaving the country. He says he wants a future position carrying legal immunity comparable to Pinochet's.
